prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first after reading all eight ballots. This is an invention that is also a discovery in the sense the statutes intend: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift limitations at once, and the original idea and the decisive early demonstration are localised to one person. Ye's group then took the concept to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and added the many-body clock work. The result has been verified by independent clocks at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST and SYRTE and by international comparisons, so it meets my test of being experimentally verified and not merely proposed. It is also a door-opening tool: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of constants and dark-matter couplings, and the likely redefinition of the second are things that could not be seen before. Four of eight members rank it in their top three and the two-name credit is the same in every ballot that lists it, which is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is precedent. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch) gave us the frequency comb on which these clocks depend, and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) honoured control of single quantum systems and ion clocks, so a sceptic can say that precision timekeeping has been rewarded twice already and the lattice clock is a refinement. A second concern is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the practical culmination is still ahead, and that Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups are outside the credited names. I take the first point seriously but think the answer is that the lattice idea is a distinct invention with its own original experiment, not a later, more beautiful version of an earlier one.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the lattice clock second but worries about overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and about the relative claim of lattice clocks versus single-ion clocks.
responses.response: I think the overlap argument is weaker than it looks. The comb is a tool that the clock uses, as a microscope uses a lens, and the 2005 citation was for the comb and laser spectroscopy, not for a clock architecture. The ion clocks of the 2012 era are limited by the number of atoms interrogated, whereas the lattice clock's key step is the magic wavelength that lets many atoms be interrogated without perturbation. That is a different original idea. I do agree that the citation must name the lattice concept explicitly so we do not appear to be rewarding generic precision. I would also ask the committee to check the priority record between Sr, Yb and Hg variants before finalising.

responses.point: Eriksson puts topological insulators first because of a clean theory-experiment loop, the 2016 prize not covering it, and the language of band topology that first-principles methods now use routinely.
responses.response: I share the view that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a serious candidate and I ranked it third, and I would not oppose it as a second choice. My difficulty is attribution rather than importance: your own ballot lists Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan as people outside the credited trio, and the HgTe experiment followed a proposal we cannot credit. The statutes allow three names, and I am not yet absolutely sure that this trio identifies the people who did the original work, because the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D topological insulators are separate discoveries. If the committee can show that the Kane-Mele Z2 step and the Molenkamp observation stand alone, I would move it up.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a general mechanism crossing condensed matter, materials and cold atoms, while acknowledging a fairness question about omitted theorists.
responses.response: The generality is a real strength, and I agree it is a better organising principle than a single measurement technique. But breadth of influence is not the same as a clean original attribution, and you yourself flag that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a real allocation concern. By contrast, the lattice-clock credit has no comparable gap in the names that decide the matter. I would rather give a prize where we can be certain about who did it first than where we must argue about who to leave out.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the lattice clock only sixth and twisted bilayer graphene seventh, noting that the redefinition of the second is still pending and that the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene is unresolved.
responses.response: I accept the second point and it is why I do not make magic-angle graphene my preferred choice even though I ranked it second: the existence of the correlated states is well established, but the mechanism is open and the field is only eight years old. On the clock I disagree. A pending redefinition of the second is a consequence of the result, not a condition for it, since the 1e-18 performance is already confirmed by independent clocks and comparisons. I would not wait for an administrative decision by the metrology community.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a textbook case of a technique that moves the limit of what can be observed, with a clean two-name credit.
responses.response: I agree and would add the caution that your own ballot raised, which is the boundary against the Hall and Wineland-era work. I think we should write the citation around the magic-wavelength lattice and the resulting accuracy, so that the record shows what is new. I also share your concern that Katori's early collaborators and the ion-clock groups are not in the credited names, and I would not claim that the two-name split has been independently verified by anyone on the committee.

uncertainties: Whether the 2005 and 2012 precedents leave room for a further precision-timekeeping prize remains a committee judgement.
Priority among lattice-clock variants (Sr, Yb, Hg) and the roles of Lemonde, Hollberg and Ludlow have not been independently verified by me.
For B039, whether the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp contributions can be separated from the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D topological insulator work.
For B035, whether the pairing mechanism must be settled before recognition.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B022. I have long-running microscopy exchanges with Tokyo and Japanese groups, but I have no stated personal tie to Katori or Ye. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, though that is relevant only to B023, which I am not proposing.
